Time to disembark?

 

People rarely think about money while sipping piña coladas and sailing to exotic destinations, but cruise-line passengers might have noticed a detail that helps explain how those companies make theirs. 

 

The hulking ships are packed and rarely idle. In an impressive logistical feat, they’ll pull into their home port in the morning and sail that afternoon with thousands of new customers and all the food and booze they can consume. Even “repositioning” a ship from the Caribbean to the Mediterranean to match regional high seasons is sold as a voyage.

 

With some ships now costing $2 billion apiece, oceangoing cruise lines have huge fixed costs. They need to be full constantly, and they have been lately.

 

That explains why the pandemic was a near-death experience for them. The three big lines, Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian, went from collectively earning $5.8 billion in 2019 to losing $50 billion over the next three fiscal years.

 

Their comeback has been remarkable. All three exceeded their prepandemic net profits last year—particularly standout Royal Caribbean. An investor who bought that stock four years ago had made triple the S&P 500’s total return by this summer.

 

Free cash flow was even more impressive. Reduced pandemic ship orders coupled with a rebound in leisure travel and stepped-up presales of onboard packages led to a windfall. And building private islands has been a masterstroke.

 

Now cruise stocks have hit their first serious bout of turbulence as growing industry capacity collides with the effects of the Iran war and some unfortunate weather, too. The cruise lines’ shares have trailed the S&P 500 by between 35% and 55% since fighting began.

 

In addition to their fixed costs, fuel is a huge variable expense. That’s happening as some cruise lines’ core middle-class customers are becoming cautious, which requires more attractive fares to keep ships full. Luxury cruise brands are doing fine. (Thank the K-shaped economy).

 

Even the booming river category, a more premium segment, looks soft as mighty waterways turned into trickles this summer in Europe. Truist analyst Patrick Scholes says that 2027 river bookings look soft.

 

In the more mass-market oceangoing market, yields—revenue per available cruise day—could face pressure toward the end of this year and in early 2027, says Scholes. Carnival’s quarterly results call on Tuesday will shed more light on that trend.

 

The current bout of softness is trifling compared with a complete halt in sailings. And high fuel prices eventually get passed on. Cruises offer decent vacation value for money, and ships tend to remain full even during recessions.

 

But the three big lines are at their prepandemic valuations on the basis of forward enterprise value to adjusted cash flow. With capacity growing, ports saturated and demand leveling off, that comes at a time when their growth prospects are subdued.

 

After a wild and rewarding ride, these ships are back to a familiar place.
